title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need?A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts

paper.title: How Many Ranks Does a Token Need? A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts
paper.abstract: Abstract Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token’s responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce Squelch , a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token’s responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein’s unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. Squelch adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, Squelch improves over LoRA by 2.2–3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8–1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: A token’s rank-one responses are a sparse signal on a noise floor (LLaMA-3.1-8B, LoRA r = 32 r{=}32 trained on commonsense reasoning). (a) Standardized responses of the trained adapter (red) against those of an untrained adapter (dashed): a Gaussian bulk plus heavy tails beyond the universal threshold. (b) The number of above-floor components per token varies with the token type. (c) Zeroing sub-floor responses after training preserves accuracy and improves held-out MMLU (right axis), whereas keeping the same number of components by top- k k or at random does not. (d) Gap between the marginal (thresholded) code and the joint sparse code as co-active value vectors become coherent (random dictionaries, exact computation); one explaining-away step closes most of it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tunes a frozen model by adding a product B ​ A BA of two thin matrices to each linear layer ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Dettmers et al., 2023 ) . Written as a sum ∑ i b i ​ a i ⊤ \sum_{i}b_{i}a_{i}^{\!\top} of r r rank-one components, the update applies all r r components to every token. Two lines of work have questioned this uniformity. Rank-allocation methods give different modules different ranks, but a module’s rank is still shared by all of its inputs ( Zhang et al., 2023c ; Ding et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Mixtures of LoRA experts route tokens among low-rank experts ( Li et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ) , and recent designs push the expert down to a single rank-one component ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . How many components fire is still fixed by hand or learned from the task loss: through a top- k k , a probability mass, a learned threshold network, or a complexity predictor ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Liu and Luo, 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . We ask the question directly: how many rank-one components does a token need? Figure 1 suggests an answer. If we collect a token’s responses u i = a ^ i ⊤ ​ x u_{i}=\hat{a}_{i}^{\!\top}x to the normalized keys of a trained LoRA, a few of them are large and the rest form a Gaussian bulk whose width matches the response of an untrained adapter, i.e. of random projections (panel a). The number of responses above this floor differs widely across tokens (panel b). The bulk also does little useful work: zeroing it after training preserves in-domain accuracy and even improves held-out retention, whereas removing the same number of components at random, or by a fixed top- k k , degrades accuracy (panel c). The bulk is cross-talk. This turns rank allocation into a detection problem, the sparse normal-means problem of signal processing ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1994 ) , and the problem comes with classical answers. One should threshold relative to a robust estimate of the noise level ( Donoho, 1995 ; Hampel, 1974 ) . The threshold can be chosen without labels by minimizing Stein’s unbiased risk estimate ( Stein, 1981 ; Donoho and Johnstone, 1995 ) . When the atoms overlap, marginal thresholding is no longer the right estimator and should give way to the joint sparse code, which iterative shrinkage approximates ( Tibshirani, 1996 ; Daubechies et al., 2004 ) . Panel (d) shows why the last point matters. As the value vectors of co-active components become coherent, the marginal code drifts far from the joint code, and a single shrinkage step removes most of the drift. We build Squelch on this view. Squelch keeps LoRA’s parameters and changes only how the rank-one components are combined for each token. It (i) squelches every response that does not clear a multiple c ℓ c_{\ell} of the token’s own noise floor, estimated by the median absolute response; (ii) sets c ℓ c_{\ell} for each module by minimizing Stein’s unbiased risk estimate over the tokens of a batch; and (iii) applies one explaining-away step that uses the Gram matrix of the value vectors to turn marginal keep-or-drop decisions into a joint one. The per-token rank is then an outcome rather than a hyperparameter: Squelch uses 8.6 of 32 components per token on average, more on numerals and less on function words, and no component is active for 8.7% of token–module pairs. Our contributions are: • A statistical view of per-token rank. Rank-one responses behave like a sparse signal on a noise floor, so choosing how many components a token uses is sparse detection (§ 1 , § 3 ). • A router-free, budget-free method. Squelch combines noise-floor thresholding, SURE-selected thresholds, and one explaining-away step, and adds no trainable parameters to LoRA (§ 3 ). • Guarantees. The squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle allocation, the SURE threshold is risk-consistent, and explaining away is a descent step toward the joint code whose error is governed by co-active coherence (§ 4 ). • Evidence. On five task families and seven backbones, Squelch outperforms ten LoRA and mixture baselines, with ablations and a controlled study that isolate each step (§ 5 , App. E ).

sections.heading: Rank allocation.
sections.text: AdaLoRA prunes singular values by an importance score ( Zhang et al., 2023c ) , SoRA gates ranks with a proximal ℓ 1 \ell_{1} step ( Ding et al., 2023 ) , and later methods allocate ranks by gradients, beam search, learned elasticity, entropy, or variational relevance ( He et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Doyle et al., 2025 ) . These methods change which modules receive rank; every input of a module shares it. Input-dependent allocation is rarer. RaNA masks ranks and neurons per input for faster inference ( Garcia et al., 2025 ) , and Flexi-LoRA predicts a rank from input complexity ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Gradient-based importance scores can also mislead ( Sawant, 2026 ) , which motivates a budget that does not depend on them.

sections.heading: Mixtures of LoRA and rank-one experts.
sections.text: MoE-LoRA methods route tokens to low-rank experts ( Zadouri et al., 2024 ; Dou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Mu et al., 2026 ) . Finer experts help: T-REX and MoDE mix rank-one experts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Ning et al., 2024 ) , SMoRA treats every rank as an expert ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , FlyLoRA routes by the top- k k responses of a frozen random down-projection ( Zou et al., 2026b ) , and MoRAM lets rank-one memories self-activate through their keys ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic MoE routing varies the number of experts through top- p p rules, null experts, ReLU gates, or confidence ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Saliencro et al., 2026 ) . Squelch shares self-routing with FlyLoRA and MoRAM but derives the number of active components from a noise model, the threshold from a risk estimate, and the combination rule from the joint sparse code.

sections.heading: Shrinkage and sparse codes in neural networks.
sections.text: Soft thresholding and iterative shrinkage are classical tools for sparse estimation ( Donoho, 1995 ; Daubechies et al., 2004 ; Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ) , and unrolled or competitive variants learn sparse codes quickly ( Rozell et al., 2008 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Monga et al., 2021 ) . In language models, thresholded activations yield activation sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ) and sparse autoencoders ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . These methods fix a sparsity level or learn a threshold; TEAL, for instance, sets one magnitude cutoff per tensor to meet a target sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Squelch instead derives the threshold from a noise model and applies it to the components of an adapter, so the cutoff follows each token’s own noise floor. Extended related work is in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Cost.
sections.text: Squelch has exactly LoRA’s parameters. Per token it adds a median over r r responses and an r × r r\times r product; per module and step it adds B ⊤ ​ B B^{\!\top}B and a power iteration on an r × r r\times r matrix. Inactive components skip the up-projection. Like every mixture of LoRA experts, the update depends on the input and cannot be merged into W 0 W_{0} .

sections.heading: Models and tasks.
sections.text: We adapt LLaMA-3.1-8B ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) and Qwen3-8B-Base ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and use Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B/14B-Base for scaling. Commonsense reasoning trains on Commonsense170K and evaluates on BoolQ, PIQA, SIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-e/c, and OBQA ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Clark et al., 2019 ; Bisk et al., 2020 ; Sap et al., 2019 ; Zellers et al., 2019 ; Sakaguchi et al., 2020 ; Clark et al., 2018 ; Mihaylov et al., 2018 ) . The domain suite trains one adapter per task: MMLU with its auxiliary training set ( Hendrycks et al., 2021a ) , ScienceQA ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , math on a 100K subset of MetaMathQA evaluated on GSM8K and MATH ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Hendrycks et al., 2021b ) , and code on a 100K subset of CodeFeedback evaluated on HumanEval and MBPP ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Austin et al., 2021 ) . GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base ( Wang et al., 2019 ; He et al., 2021 ) , joint multi-task training, and forgetting are reported in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: Single adapters: LoRA, DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024b ) , AdaLoRA, and GoRA. Mixtures: HydraLoRA, MixLoRA, AdaMoLE, LD-MoLE, SMoRA, and FlyLoRA. All adapters target the seven projection matrices and are matched to LoRA with r = 32 r{=}32 in trainable parameters, except FlyLoRA, whose frozen down-projection halves them, and SMoRA, whose router adds a third. Rank-wise baselines use 32 32 components with k = 8 k{=}8 active, the configuration of FlyLoRA ( Zou et al., 2026b ) .

sections.heading: Implementation.
sections.text: Squelch uses r = 32 r{=}32 , α = 64 \alpha{=}64 , a 5 % 5\% dense warm-up, SURE every 20 20 steps with EMA 0.9 0.9 , and cap c U = 2 ​ log ⁡ 32 c_{\mathrm{U}}{=}\sqrt{2\log 32} , with identical settings for every task and backbone. All methods share the optimizer, schedule, and data; we report the mean of three seeds (standard deviations and full settings in Appendices G and H ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Main Results
sections.text: Figure 3: Where Squelch spends rank (LLaMA-3.1-8B). (a) Mean active rank by layer and module: FFN projections in the middle and upper layers use the most components. (b) Mean active rank by task: math and code use more components than knowledge and science. (c) SURE-selected multiples c ℓ c_{\ell} ( ± \pm s.d. across layers) stay below the universal cap and are lower for FFN modules. (d) Explaining away inhibits and recruits the most components in FFN modules, where co-active values are most coherent (right axis). (b) Accuracy vs. mean active rank: Squelch with a target rank (budgeted variant), top- k k variants, and LoRA; the star is SURE’s choice. (c) Accuracy of global fixed multiples c c relative to the best one; stars mark per-module SURE. (d) Gain over LoRA across Qwen3 sizes; numbers give Squelch ’s mean active rank. Squelch attains the best average in all four settings (Tables 1 and 2 ). On commonsense reasoning it reaches 87.04 on LLaMA-3.1-8B and 89.28 on Qwen3-8B, + 2.64 +2.64 and + 2.18 +2.18 over LoRA and + 0.93 +0.93 and + 0.77 +0.77 over the strongest baseline, FlyLoRA. On the domain suite, the margins over FlyLoRA are + 1.19 +1.19 and + 0.75 +0.75 . Three patterns stand out. First, input-adaptive methods beat input-shared ones at comparable parameter budgets. LD-MoLE, SMoRA, and FlyLoRA all exceed AdaLoRA and GoRA, so where rank is spent matters more than how it is divided among modules. Second, Squelch is better than the rank-wise mixtures at a similar active rank ( 8.6 8.6 vs. 8 8 ) and without a router: the gain comes from choosing which and how many components fire, not from activating more. Third, gains concentrate on tasks that require composition, namely ARC-c, WinoGrande, OBQA, GSM8K, and code. On MMLU, whose adaptation is closer to a uniform shift, FlyLoRA and Squelch are within 0.1 0.1 on LLaMA, and on HellaSwag SMoRA is best on Qwen3; both are near saturation. The improvements exceed three seed standard deviations in every setting (Table 9 ).

sections.heading: Rank follows the input.
sections.text: Per-token ranks range from 0 0 to over 20 20 (Figure 7 ). Numerals and operators use 11.8 11.8 components on average, content words 9.4 9.4 , function words 5.3 5.3 , and punctuation 3.9 3.9 . Across tasks, math and code use the most (Figure 3 b). Out of domain, the squelch closes more often: on MMLU prompts, a commonsense adapter leaves 21.4% of token–module pairs without active components, against 8.7% in domain. This selectivity explains the smaller forgetting of Squelch ( − 1.13 -1.13 vs. − 3.87 -3.87 points for LoRA on held-out benchmarks; Table 12 ).

sections.heading: Budgets emerge per module.
sections.text: SURE assigns lower multiples, and thus more components, to FFN projections than to attention queries and keys (Figure 3 c), and the resulting ranks peak in the upper-middle layers (Figure 3 a). The selected multiples stabilize within the first tenth of training (Figure 6 ) and stay below the universal cap everywhere, so the cap acts only as a safeguard.

sections.heading: Explaining away acts where values overlap.
sections.text: Explaining away removes 5 5 – 17 % 17\% of first-pass components and recruits 8 8 – 26 % 26\% more, most in FFN modules, where the values of co-active components are most coherent (Figure 3 d). Restricting it to attention modules recovers 0.21 0.21 of its 0.61 0.61 -point gain, and restricting it to FFN modules recovers 0.49 0.49 , in line with Proposition 4 (d). A controlled synthetic study with a known per-input rank (Appendix E ) shows the same division of labour: the squelch alone is conservative, and explaining away makes the active count track the true rank.

sections.heading: Larger dictionaries keep helping.
sections.text: Because each token uses only what it needs, Squelch converts a larger dictionary into accuracy without a larger per-token rank budget. From r = 8 r{=}8 to 128 128 it gains 2.6 2.6 points while its mean active rank grows only from 2.9 2.9 to 15.8 15.8 ; LoRA saturates beyond r = 32 r{=}32 and the top- k k mixtures around r = 64 r{=}64 (Figure 4 a).

sections.heading: The SURE choice sits at the knee.
sections.text: With a target average rank enforced by a dual variable, Squelch dominates top- k k rules at every budget, including its own top- k k variant (Figure 4 b). The budget-free SURE point ( k ¯ = 8.6 \bar{k}{=}8.6 ) lies at the knee of this frontier, and per-module SURE beats the best global multiple found by grid search on three tasks (Figure 4 c). The budget is thus found, not tuned.

sections.heading: Scale and cost.
sections.text: The gain over LoRA persists from 0.6 0.6 B to 14 14 B parameters, and the mean active rank grows slowly with model size (Figure 4 d). Squelch trains 5 % 5\% slower than unmerged LoRA and adds 5 % 5\% to inference latency, less than mixtures with learned routers (Table 16 ).

sections.heading: Beyond single tasks.
sections.text: The same selectivity helps when tasks share one adapter. Trained jointly on the six domain tasks, Squelch loses only 0.47 points relative to separate adapters, against 1.50 for LoRA and 0.85 for FlyLoRA (Table 11 ), because tokens of different tasks clear the floor on different components. On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, it raises the average from 88.41 (LoRA) to 89.71 with 2.9 2.9 of 8 8 components active per token (Table 10 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: How many rank-one components a token needs is a detection problem: a token’s responses to a LoRA dictionary are a sparse signal on a noise floor. Squelch answers it with three classical steps, a robust per-token floor, a threshold chosen by unbiased risk, and one explaining-away step toward the joint sparse code. It needs neither a router nor a rank budget, adds no parameters to LoRA, and improves over strong single-adapter and mixture baselines across tasks and scales. The same view applies wherever a model combines many small components per input, including mixtures of full experts and sparse autoencoders.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: The noise model is an idealization: responses of irrelevant components are only approximately Gaussian, and the median estimate is biased upward when many components are active (Appendix C ), which SURE compensates only in part. Explaining away is a single proximal step; it closes part of the gap to the joint code, and our synthetic study shows that it resolves redundancy in the code rather than disentangling the dictionary itself. Like every input-dependent adapter, Squelch cannot be merged into the backbone, and it adds a small inference overhead. Our experiments cover decoder models up to 14B parameters and one encoder, supervised fine-tuning, and English benchmarks; reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, multilingual adaptation, and larger models remain to be tested.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: Squelch is a general fine-tuning method and inherits the risks of the models and data to which it is applied, including biases in instruction data and the lower cost of specializing models for harmful uses. All datasets are public and used under their licenses; no human subjects or personal data are involved. Because Squelch leaves out-of-domain tokens closer to the frozen model, it reduces but does not remove the risk that fine-tuning erodes safety behavior; such behavior should be evaluated after adaptation. AI assistants were used for language editing and for checking LaTeX; every reference was checked against its primary record.

sections.heading: LoRA and its reparameterizations.
sections.text: LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) and its quantized form ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) made low-rank updates the default for adapting large models. Later work changes the parameterization or the optimization of the update. DoRA separates magnitude from direction ( Liu et al., 2024b ) ; PiSSA initializes from principal singular directions ( Meng et al., 2024 ) ; LoRA-GA and LoRA-Pro align the low-rank gradient with the full one ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2025a ) ; rsLoRA and LoRA+ correct the scale and learning rates of the two factors ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ; Hayou et al., 2024 ) ; VeRA shares frozen random factors ( Kopiczko et al., 2024 ) ; MELoRA and MoRA raise the rank of the update at a fixed parameter count ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024b ) . Two findings are relevant to our noise-floor view. LoRA’s down-projection changes much less than its up-projection and can even be frozen at random initialization ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; the responses A ​ x Ax of most components therefore stay close to random projections of the input, which is the floor that Squelch estimates. LoRA also forgets less than full fine-tuning ( Biderman et al., 2024 ) , but its updates introduce new high-variance directions that account for much of the forgetting ( Shuttleworth et al., 2025 ; Xie and Alanwar, 2026 ) . Squelch leaves the tokens on which no component clears the floor on the frozen path.

sections.heading: Rank allocation.
sections.text: Static allocation gives each module its own rank. AdaLoRA prunes singular values by sensitivity ( Zhang et al., 2023c ) , SoRA gates ranks with a proximal ℓ 1 \ell_{1} step, i.e. soft thresholding of a gate vector that is shared by all inputs ( Ding et al., 2023 ) , and DyLoRA and IncreLoRA train nested or growing ranks ( Valipour et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023a ) . ALoRA and AutoLoRA learn allocations by ablation scores or meta-learning ( Liu et al., 2024c ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Recent methods use gradient information ( He et al., 2025 ) , beam search over ranks ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , elastic pruning and growth ( Chang et al., 2025 ) , differentiable module selection ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , hypernetworks ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , entropy ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , per-expert ranks for MoE backbones ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , information-bottleneck filtering ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) , variational relevance ( Doyle et al., 2025 ) , integrated gradients with uncertainty ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , calibration-time gradient variance ( Sathyavageeswaran, 2026 ) , or nested representations that support several ranks at test time ( Modoranu et al., 2026 ) . Gradient-based importance can fail, for example under reinforcement learning ( Sawant, 2026 ) . All of these methods fix a module’s rank for every input. RaNA allocates ranks and neurons per input to speed up inference ( Garcia et al., 2025 ) , and Flexi-LoRA predicts a rank from the complexity of the input ( Li et al., 2026 ) ; Squelch obtains the per-token rank from the responses themselves and requires neither a predictor nor a budget.

sections.heading: Mixtures of LoRA experts.
sections.text: LoRAMoE, MixLoRA, MoLE, and MoLA route tokens or layers to LoRA experts ( Dou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Gao et al., 2024 ) ; HydraLoRA shares the down-projection across asymmetric heads ( Tian et al., 2024 ) ; MoSLoRA mixes subspaces ( Wu et al., 2024a ) ; and extremely light variants mix vectors or rank-one factors ( Zadouri et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2023 ) . Multi-task variants target task conflicts ( Liu et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . Routing has been refined with hybrid, learnable, or dynamic rules ( Li et al., 2025a ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ; Liu and Luo, 2024 ) , orthogonality or diversity among experts ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , communication between experts ( Mu et al., 2026 ) , rotational gates ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , singular-value alignment ( Fan et al., 2025 ) , and expert-aware adaptation of MoE backbones ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Other designs place experts in the attention projections ( Li et al., 2025b ) , partition adapters into blocks with adaptive routing ( Barazandeh et al., 2026 ) , compose frozen tensor-train experts ( Kunwar et al., 2025 ) , or remove the discrete router so that the mixture can be merged ( Han et al., 2025 ) . Routing alone does not remove interference inside a shared adapter subspace ( Chowdhury et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Rank-one experts.
sections.text: Fine-grained experts are the closest line of work. T-REX combines rank-one experts with semantic priors for the router ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) ; MoDE shares the down-projection and routes over rank-one “dyadic” experts ( Ning et al., 2024 ) ; SMoRA shows that routing among several LoRAs equals rank partitioning within one LoRA and treats every rank as an expert with a learned router and top- k k ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) ; FlyLoRA freezes a sparse random down-projection whose top- k k responses select the active columns of the up-projection, an implicit router ( Zou et al., 2026b ) ; and MoRAM views rank-one adapters as key–value memories that self-activate by their keys ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Rank-one experts also appear as orthogonal experts obtained from the singular vectors of pretrained weights ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) , as reusable rank-wise experts in federated fine-tuning ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and as an expert pool inside a single LoRA for continual learning ( Fa et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026a ) . Their view of self-routing through each component’s own key goes back to reading feed-forward layers as key–value memories ( Geva et al., 2021 ) . Squelch keeps self-routing and adds what these methods fix by hand: how many components fire (a noise-calibrated threshold instead of top- k k ), how the threshold is set (an unbiased risk estimate instead of a budget), and how co-active components combine (a joint code instead of a sum).

sections.heading: Dynamic routing in sparse MoE.
sections.text: Sparse MoE layers route each token to a fixed number of experts ( Shazeer et al., 2017 ; Fedus et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2024a ; Dai et al., 2024 ) , or let experts choose tokens ( Zhou et al., 2022 ) , with auxiliary or bias-based load balancing ( Wang et al., 2024a ) . Several methods let the number of experts vary: top- p p routing ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and its sparsity-controlled variant ( Jin et al., 2026 ) , thresholds on router scores ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , null or zero-computation experts ( Zeng et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) , top-any gating ( Guo et al., 2025 ) , ReLU routers with an adaptive ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , and confidence-adaptive routing for MoE-LoRA ( Saliencro et al., 2026 ) . These methods learn a router and control sparsity through a target or a penalty. The squelch has no router and sets sparsity from the responses’ own noise level.

sections.heading: Activation sparsity and sparse autoencoders.
sections.text: Contextual and ReLU-induced sparsity speed up inference ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Mirzadeh et al., 2024 ) . CATS and TEAL threshold hidden states at magnitudes chosen for a target sparsity ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) , R-Sparse and La RoSA combine sparsity with low-rank or rotated bases ( Zhang et al., 2025c ; Liu et al., 2025b ) , and recent methods allocate sparsity across projections by heavy-tail statistics or weight awareness ( Hou et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Sparse autoencoders learn overcomplete dictionaries of model activations with ReLU, TopK, JumpReLU, or BatchTopK codes ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ; Bussmann et al., 2024 ) , and Monet builds monosemantic experts into the architecture ( Park et al., 2025 ) . Squelch treats the adapter itself as a small dictionary and picks the sparsity of each token’s code by a noise model rather than a target.

sections.heading: Shrinkage, sparse coding, and unrolling.
sections.text: Soft thresholding at the universal level is minimax up to a logarithmic factor ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1994 ; Donoho, 1995 ) . Stein’s unbiased risk estimate ( Stein, 1981 ) makes the threshold data-adaptive ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1995 ) , and the median absolute deviation is the standard robust scale estimate ( Hampel, 1974 ) . For overlapping dictionaries, the LASSO ( Tibshirani, 1996 ) is solved by iterative shrinkage ( Daubechies et al., 2004 ; Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ) , whose accuracy depends on the coherence of the atoms ( Tropp, 2004 ) . Sparse coding with competition between units ( Olshausen and Field, 1996 ; Rozell et al., 2008 ) and unrolled shrinkage networks ( Chen et al., 2018 ; Monga et al., 2021 ) learn such codes efficiently, and white-box transformers insert a shrinkage step into each block ( Yu et al., 2023 ) . Explaining away in Squelch is one such step, with the inhibition tied to the adapter’s value dictionary rather than learned.

sections.heading: Why a threshold learned by the task loss collapses.
sections.text: For active components, ∂ z i / ∂ τ = − sign ⁡ ( u i ) \partial z_{i}/\partial\tau=-\mathrm{sign}(u_{i}) , so lowering τ \tau enlarges every active coefficient and activates new components; both enlarge the set of functions the adapter can fit. Gradient descent on τ \tau therefore tends to decrease it until the code is nearly dense, as the ablation shows ( k ¯ = 27.9 \bar{k}=27.9 ). ReLU routers face the same pressure and need an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty with an adaptive coefficient to keep their sparsity ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . SURE avoids this because it measures the error with respect to the signal in the responses, not the fit to the training loss.

sections.heading: Soft versus hard thresholds.
sections.text: Hard thresholding keeps u i u_{i} unchanged above τ \tau and makes the layer discontinuous at the threshold, so a small change of the input can switch a component with its full magnitude. Soft thresholding is continuous and 1-Lipschitz in u u , which keeps training stable; JumpReLU autoencoders need straight-through estimators to train hard thresholds ( Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . Hard thresholds lose 0.19 0.19 points (Table 3 ).

sections.heading: Relation to competitive sparse coding.
sections.text: Explaining away is one step of the locally competitive algorithm ( Rozell et al., 2008 ) . The feed-forward drive is the response u u , the lateral inhibition is the normalized value Gram M M , and the step starts from the thresholded drive rather than from zero. Unlike LISTA ( Gregor and LeCun, 2010 ; Chen et al., 2018 ) , Squelch does not learn the inhibition: it is tied to the synthesis dictionary B B , so Squelch keeps LoRA’s parameter count and its inhibition stays consistent with the update it synthesizes.

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: Table 5 and Figure 5 support three conclusions and qualify a fourth. (1) Input-adaptive rank matters. A dense student cannot gate and has the largest error. Fixed top- k k students are better but cannot adapt to the true rank, and a larger k k hurts because it adds floor components to low-rank inputs. (2) The squelch alone is conservative. Without explaining away, the SURE threshold keeps about three components per input regardless of the true rank (Spearman 0.37 0.37 and 0.60 0.60 ). (3) Explaining away makes the active count track the true rank (Spearman 0.66 0.66 and 0.84 0.84 ) and gives the lowest error when the teacher’s values are coherent ( 0.240 0.240 vs. 0.293 0.293 ). With orthogonal values the two variants are on par. The mean error of the full method is higher here only because one seed converged to a poor solution ( 0.420 0.420 ); its median error is lower ( 0.280 0.280 vs. 0.314 0.314 ). (4) Explaining away does not disentangle the dictionary. Starting from 16 16 near-duplicate pairs, the pairs drift apart without explaining away (mean | cos | |\cos| 0.17 after training) but stay closer with it (0.39), and the effective rank of co-active values is lower (participation ratio over active count 0.33 vs. 0.87). Explaining away makes redundancy harmless in the code, since redundant components share rather than duplicate their contribution, so training has less reason to separate them. A penalty on co-activation-weighted coherence restores separation but reduces error only when the dictionary is scarce (Table 6 ). We therefore describe explaining away as joint credit assignment rather than as a disentangling regularizer. No EA EA EA+pen. sections.heading: Layer.
sections.text: Squelch replaces the forward pass of a LoRA module and keeps its parameters and initialization ( A A Kaiming-uniform, B = 0 B=0 ). Responses are computed in bfloat16, and the median, thresholds, and explaining-away step in float32. With B = 0 B=0 at initialization, G = 0 G=0 and M M is defined as 0 0 , so explaining away switches on gradually as the values grow. The step size uses ten power iterations on the cosine Gram with a floor of λ max ≥ 1 \lambda_{\max}\geq 1 . Gradients flow through u u , z 0 z^{0} , z z , and G G ; σ ^ \hat{\sigma} , c ℓ c_{\ell} , and η \eta are treated as constants.

sections.heading: SURE controller.
sections.text: Every 20 20 steps and for each module, we standardize the responses of up to 4,096 4{,}096 tokens of the current batch, evaluate SURE on 65 65 equally spaced multiples in [ 0 , c U ] [0,c_{\mathrm{U}}] , and take the minimizer. If the SureShrink sparsity statistic 1 N ​ r ​ ∑ ( v 2 − 1 ) ≤ ( log 2 ⁡ N ​ r ) 3 / 2 / N ​ r \frac{1}{Nr}\sum(v^{2}-1)\leq(\log_{2}Nr)^{3/2}/\sqrt{Nr} indicates no signal, the controller returns c U c_{\mathrm{U}} ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1995 ) . The multiple is smoothed with an EMA of 0.9 0.9 and ramped linearly from zero during the first 5 % 5\% of steps. The controller costs O ⁡ ( 65 ​ N ​ r ) O(65\,Nr) operations per module per update, less than 0.2 % 0.2\% of the step time.

sections.heading: Budgeted variant.
sections.text: For deployments that need a fixed average rank, the controller is replaced by dual ascent on the constraint 𝔼 ​ | supp ​ z | = k ¯ \mathbb{E}|\mathrm{supp}z|=\bar{k} : c ℓ ← c ℓ + κ ⁡ ( k ^ ℓ − k ¯ ) c_{\ell}\leftarrow c_{\ell}+\kappa(\hat{k}_{\ell}-\bar{k}) with κ = 0.01 \kappa=0.01 . This variant produces the curve in Figure 4 b.

sections.heading: Inference.
sections.text: The update depends on the input and cannot be merged into W 0 W_{0} . We batch the down-projection as in LoRA, compute the code, and apply the up-projection only to the active columns of each token through a gathered matrix product; for batch sizes above 16 16 , a dense product with the sparse code is equally fast.

sections.heading: Prompts.
sections.text: Commonsense and math use the instruction template of LLM-Adapters ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2025 ) : “Below is an instruction that describes a task. Write a response that appropriately completes the request. ### Instruction: {question} ### Response:”. For multiple-choice tasks, the instruction lists the options, and the answer is the option name extracted from the response. Code uses the instruction–response format of CodeFeedback ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) ; the HumanEval and MBPP prompts contain the function signature and docstring, or the problem statement and test examples. MMLU and ScienceQA present the question with its lettered options and ask for the letter.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: Commonsense tasks use the LLM-Adapters prompts and answer extraction with greedy decoding. MMLU and ScienceQA report accuracy with zero-shot prompts after fine-tuning. GSM8K and MATH report exact match of the final answer, and HumanEval and MBPP report pass@1 with greedy decoding. All methods share prompts, decoding, and answer extraction.

sections.heading: Is the squelch just a ReLU gate on LoRA ranks?
sections.text: No. A ReLU gate, or SoRA’s proximal gate ( Ding et al., 2023 ) , thresholds at a fixed or learned level that is shared by all inputs, and its sparsity is set by a penalty weight. The squelch thresholds each token relative to that token’s own noise level, which makes the active set invariant to the token’s norm (Proposition 1 (ii)), and it sets the multiple by an unbiased risk estimate, without a penalty weight or a target sparsity. Table 3 shows that both choices matter: a per-layer scale loses 0.46 0.46 and a threshold learned by the task loss collapses toward a dense code.

sections.heading: Why not learn a router, as mixture methods do?
sections.text: A router adds parameters, must be balanced, and learns from a loss that rewards activating more components. Squelch routes through the keys that the adapter already has and decides the number of active components with a label-free statistic ( Peng et al., 2024 ) . At matched average rank it outperforms routed rank-wise mixtures (Table 18 ).

sections.heading: Are the responses really Gaussian?
sections.text: Only approximately. The median estimate needs only a symmetric bulk and at most half of the components carrying signal, and SURE needs only an approximately Gaussian bulk near the threshold. Heavier-tailed noise ( Kunstner et al., 2024 ) would make the universal cap too permissive, but SURE’s multiples stay well below the cap (Figure 3 c), and the sensitivity to the cap is small (Table 15 ).

sections.heading: What happens when a token needs many components?
sections.text: The median estimate then errs upward (Appendix C ), which raises the threshold, so the squelch is conservative for such tokens. Explaining away partly compensates by recruiting complementary components (Figure 3 d). A larger dictionary helps more than a lower threshold (Figure 4 a).

sections.heading: Does Squelch save compute?
sections.text: Not much at training time. The down-projection must be computed for all components to evaluate the responses, and LoRA’s cost is small to begin with. Its purpose is accuracy and selectivity at LoRA’s parameter count. At inference, inactive components skip the up-projection, but merged LoRA remains faster ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) (Table 16 ).

sections.heading: Is the comparison fair to the mixtures?
sections.text: All methods have the same target modules, data, optimizer, schedule, and evaluation, and all but FlyLoRA and SMoRA are matched to LoRA’s parameter count. FlyLoRA has fewer trainable parameters by design, and SMoRA has more because of its router. Learning rates were tuned per method (Appendix G ).

sections.heading: Can Squelch be combined with other LoRA improvements?
sections.text: Yes. The squelch only changes how components are combined per token, so it composes with initialization schemes, magnitude–direction decompositions, and optimizer corrections ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Hayou et al., 2024 ) . We have not tested these combinations.

sections.heading: Why a noise model instead of a router.
sections.text: A router must learn from the task loss both where to send a token and how many components to use, and the task loss rewards using more. Squelch separates the two questions. Where to send a token is answered by the keys, as in other self-routing designs ( Zou et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . How many components it needs is answered by comparing each response with what an irrelevant component would produce. The second question has a label-free, statistically grounded answer, and the rest of the method follows from it: a robust scale, an unbiased risk, and a joint code.

sections.heading: What the noise floor is.
sections.text: The floor is the response of components whose keys are unrelated to the token. Because LoRA’s down-projection moves little from its random initialization ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) , most keys remain close to random directions, and their responses are close to Gaussian with a scale proportional to ‖ x ‖ \|x\| ; this is why the bulk in Figure 1 a matches an untrained adapter. As training proceeds, keys that align with a token’s directions leave the bulk, and the squelch lets exactly those through. The MAD scale makes the rule invariant to the token’s norm (Proposition 1 (ii)), which matters because norms vary widely across tokens and layers ( Sun et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: What explaining away does and does not do.
sections.text: Explaining away turns marginal decisions into a joint one: it removes double counting among overlapping values and recruits components that are needed only together. It does not make the dictionary itself less redundant, and our synthetic study shows that near-duplicate components can stay aligned when it is used (Appendix E ). Methods that disentangle co-activated components through a regularizer target a different quantity, the coherence of the dictionary. In our experiments, such a penalty partially substitutes for explaining away but adds nothing on top of it (Table 3 ), and helps only when the dictionary is too small for the task (Table 6 ).

sections.heading: When Squelch helps less.
sections.text: Tasks whose adaptation is close to a uniform shift, such as MMLU in our experiments, gain little from input-dependent rank, because most tokens need the same few components. Very small dictionaries ( r ≤ 8 r\leq 8 ) leave little room for selection. Settings that require merging the adapter into the backbone for zero-overhead inference should use LoRA, or distill the squelched adapter into a merged one ( Bensaid et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Extensions.
sections.text: The same statistical view applies to other ways of combining many small components per input: routing among full experts, where the responses are router logits; sparse autoencoders, where SURE could set per-feature thresholds without a sparsity target; and continual learning, where tokens that no old component answers could trigger new components. Applying the squelch in reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, where gradient-based allocation has been reported to fail ( Sawant, 2026 ) , is a natural next test.

sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: Squelch makes fine-tuning more parameter- and compute-efficient and leaves out-of-domain inputs closer to the base model. The first lowers the cost of adaptation for everyone, including malicious users; the second reduces, but does not remove, the risk that fine-tuning degrades safety behavior ( Qi et al., 2024 ) .

A Noise-Floor Squelch for Rank-One LoRA Experts Mei Okonkwo Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Owen Castellanos Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Ingrid Solberg Affiliation: Delft University of Technology Yusuf Demirel Affiliation: University of Edinburgh Abstract Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token’s responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce Squelch , a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token’s responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein’s unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. Squelch adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, Squelch improves over LoRA by 2.2–3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8–1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average. 1 Introduction Figure 1: A token’s rank-one responses are a sparse signal on a noise floor (LLaMA-3.1-8B, LoRA r = 32 r{=}32 trained on commonsense reasoning). (a) Standardized responses of the trained adapter (red) against those of an untrained adapter (dashed): a Gaussian bulk plus heavy tails beyond the universal threshold. (b) The number of above-floor components per token varies with the token type. (c) Zeroing sub-floor responses after training preserves accuracy and improves held-out MMLU (right axis), whereas keeping the same number of components by top- k k or at random does not. (d) Gap between the marginal (thresholded) code and the joint sparse code as co-active value vectors become coherent (random dictionaries, exact computation); one explaining-away step closes most of it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tunes a frozen model by adding a product B ​ A BA of two thin matrices to each linear layer ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Dettmers et al., 2023 ) . Written as a sum ∑ i b i ​ a i ⊤ \sum_{i}b_{i}a_{i}^{\!\top} of r r rank-one components, the update applies all r r components to every token. Two lines of work have questioned this uniformity. Rank-allocation methods give different modules different ranks, but a module’s rank is still shared by all of its inputs ( Zhang et al., 2023c ; Ding et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Mixtures of LoRA experts route tokens among low-rank experts ( Li et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ) , and recent designs push the expert down to a single rank-one component ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . How many components fire is still fixed by hand or learned from the task loss: through a top- k k , a probability mass, a learned threshold network, or a complexity predictor ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Liu and Luo, 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . We ask the question directly: how many rank-one components does a token need? Figure 1 suggests an answer. If we collect a token’s responses u i = a ^ i ⊤ ​ x u_{i}=\hat{a}_{i}^{\!\top}x to the normalized keys of a trained LoRA, a few of them are large and the rest form a Gaussian bulk whose width matches the response of an untrained adapter, i.e. of random projections (panel a). The number of responses above this floor differs widely across tokens (panel b). The bulk also does little useful work: zeroing it after training preserves in-domain accuracy and even improves held-out retention, whereas removing the same number of components at random, or by a fixed top- k k , degrades accuracy (panel c). The bulk is cross-talk. This turns rank allocation into a detection problem, the sparse normal-means problem of signal processing ( Donoho and Johnstone, 1994 ) , and the problem comes with classical answers. One should threshold relative to a robust estimate of the noise level ( Donoho, 1995 ; Hampel, 1974 ) . The threshold can be chosen without labels by minimizing Stein’s unbiased risk estimate ( Stein, 1981 ; Donoho and Johnstone, 1995 ) . When the atoms overlap, marginal thresholding is no longer the right estimator and should give way to the joint sparse code, which iterative shrinkage approximates ( Tibshirani, 1996 ; Daubechies et al., 2004 ) . Panel (d) shows why the last point matters. As the value vectors of co-active components become coherent, the marginal code drifts far from the joint code, and a single shrinkage step removes most of the drift. We build Squelch on this view. Squelch keeps LoRA’s parameters and changes only how the rank-one components are combined for each token. It (i) squelches every response that does not clear a multiple c ℓ c_{\ell} of the token’s own noise floor, estimated by the median absolute response; (ii) sets c ℓ c_{\ell} for each module by minimizing Stein’s unbiased risk estimate over the tokens of a batch; and (iii) applies one explaining-away step that uses the Gram matrix of the value vectors to turn marginal keep-or-drop decisions into a joint one. The per-token rank is then an outcome rather than a hyperparameter: Squelch uses 8.6 of 32 components per token on average, more on numerals and less on function words, and no component is active for 8.7% of token–module pairs. Our contributions are: • A statistical view of per-token rank. Rank-one responses behave like a sparse signal on a noise floor, so choosing how many components a token uses is sparse detection (§ 1 , § 3 ). • A router-free, budget-free method. Squelch combines noise-floor thresholding, SURE-selected thresholds, and one explaining-away step, and adds no trainable parameters to LoRA (§ 3 ). • Guarantees. The squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle allocation, the SURE threshold is risk-consistent, and explaining away is a descent step toward the joint code whose error is governed by co-active coherence (§ 4 ). • Evidence. On five task families and seven backbones, Squelch outperforms ten LoRA and mixture baselines, with ablations and a controlled study that isolate each step (§ 5 , App. E ). 2 Related Work Figure 2: Squelch in one adapted layer. The token’s responses to r r unit-norm keys are squelched at a multiple c ℓ c_{\ell} of the token’s own noise floor, where c ℓ c_{\ell} is chosen per module by Stein’s unbiased risk estimate. One explaining-away step on the value Gram B ⊤ ​ B B^{\!\top}\!B turns the marginal code into a joint one. The surviving components form the token’s update, so its rank varies per token. Squelch uses LoRA’s parameters A , B A,B and adds none. Rank allocation. AdaLoRA prunes singular values by an importance score ( Zhang et al., 2023c ) , SoRA gates ranks with a proximal ℓ 1 \ell_{1} step ( Ding et al., 2023 ) , and later methods allocate ranks by gradients, beam search, learned elasticity, entropy, or variational relevance ( He et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Doyle et al., 2025 ) . These methods change which modules receive rank; every input of a module shares it. Input-dependent allocation is rarer. RaNA masks ranks and neurons per input for faster inference ( Garcia et al., 2025 ) , and Flexi-LoRA predicts a rank from input complexity ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Gradient-based importance scores can also mislead ( Sawant, 2026 ) , which motivates a budget that does not depend on them. Mixtures of LoRA and rank-one experts. MoE-LoRA methods route tokens to low-rank experts ( Zadouri et al., 2024 ; Dou et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Zhuang et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2025 ; Mu et al., 2026 ) . Finer experts help: T-REX and MoDE mix rank-one experts ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Ning et al., 2024 ) , SMoRA treats every rank as an expert ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , FlyLoRA routes by the top- k k responses of a frozen random down-projection ( Zou et al., 2026b ) , and MoRAM lets rank-one memories self-activate through their keys ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Dynamic MoE routing varies the number of experts through top- p p rules, null experts, ReLU gates, or confidence ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Saliencro et al., 2026 ) . Squelch shares self-routing with FlyLoRA and MoRAM but derives the number of active components from a noise model, the threshold from a risk estimate, and the combination rule from the joint sparse code. Shrinkage and sparse codes in neural networks. Soft thresholding and iterative shrinkage are classical tools for sparse estimation ( Donoho, 1995 ; Daubechies et al., 2004 ; Beck and Teboulle, 2009 ) , and unrolled or competitive variants learn sparse codes quickly ( Rozell et al., 2008 ; Chen et al., 2018 ; Monga et al., 2021 ) . In language models, thresholded activations yield activation sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ) and sparse autoencoders ( Cunningham et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . These methods fix a sparsity level or learn a threshold; TEAL, for instance, sets one magnitude cutoff per tensor to meet a target sparsity ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Squelch instead derives the threshold from a noise model and applies it to the components of an adapter, so the cutoff follows each token’s own noise floor. Per-token ranks range from 0 0 to over 20 20 (Figure 7 ). Numerals and operators use 11.8 11.8 components on average, content words 9.4 9.4 , function words 5.3 5.3 , and punctuation 3.9 3.9 . Across tasks, math and code use the most (Figure 3 b). Out of domain, the squelch closes more often: on MMLU prompts, a commonsense adapter leaves 21.4% of token–module pairs without active components, against 8.7% in domain. This selectivity explains the smaller forgetting of Squelch ( − 1.13 -1.13 vs. − 3.87 -3.87 points for LoRA on held-out benchmarks; Table 12 ). Budgets emerge per module. SURE assigns lower multiples, and thus more components, to FFN projections than to attention queries and keys (Figure 3 c), and the resulting ranks peak in the upper-middle layers (Figure 3 a). The selected multiples stabilize within the first tenth of training (Figure 6 ) and stay below the universal cap everywhere, so the cap acts only as a safeguard. Explaining away acts where values overlap. Explaining away removes 5 5 – 17 % 17\% of first-pass components and recruits 8 8 – 26 % 26\% more, most in FFN modules, where the values of co-active components are most coherent (Figure 3 d). Restricting it to attention modules recovers 0.21 0.21 of its 0.61 0.61 -point gain, and restricting it to FFN modules recovers 0.49 0.49 , in line with Proposition 4 (d). A controlled synthetic study with a known per-input rank (Appendix E ) shows the same division of labour: the squelch alone is conservative, and explaining away makes the active count track the true rank. 5.5 Capacity, Budget, and Scaling Larger dictionaries keep helping. Because each token uses only what it needs, Squelch converts a larger dictionary into accuracy without a larger per-token rank budget. From r = 8 r{=}8 to 128 128 it gains 2.6 2.6 points while its mean active rank grows only from 2.9 2.9 to 15.8 15.8 ; LoRA saturates beyond r = 32 r{=}32 and the top- k k mixtures around r = 64 r{=}64 (Figure 4 a). The SURE choice sits at the knee. With a target average rank enforced by a dual variable, Squelch dominates top- k k rules at every budget, including its own top- k k variant (Figure 4 b). The budget-free SURE point ( k ¯ = 8.6 \bar{k}{=}8.6 ) lies at the knee of this frontier, and per-module SURE beats the best global multiple found by grid search on three tasks (Figure 4 c). The budget is thus found, not tuned. Scale and cost. The gain over LoRA persists from 0.6 0.6 B to 14 14 B parameters, and the mean active rank grows slowly with model size (Figure 4 d). Squelch trains 5 % 5\% slower than unmerged LoRA and adds 5 % 5\% to inference latency, less than mixtures with learned routers (Table 16 ). Beyond single tasks. The same selectivity helps when tasks share one adapter. Trained jointly on the six domain tasks, Squelch loses only 0.47 points relative to separate adapters, against 1.50 for LoRA and 0.85 for FlyLoRA (Table 11 ), because tokens of different tasks clear the floor on different components. On GLUE with DeBERTaV3-base, it raises the average from 88.41 (LoRA) to 89.71 with 2.9 2.9 of 8 8 components active per token (Table 10 ). 6 Conclusion How many rank-one components a token needs is a detection problem: a token’s responses to a LoRA dictionary are a sparse signal on a noise floor. Squelch answers it with three classical steps, a robust per-token floor, a threshold chosen by unbiased risk, and one explaining-away step toward the joint sparse code. It needs neither a router nor a rank budget, adds no parameters to LoRA, and improves over strong single-adapter and mixture baselines across tasks and scales. The same view applies wherever a model combines many small components per input, including mixtures of full experts and sparse autoencoders. Limitations The noise model is an idealization: responses of irrelevant components are only approximately Gaussian, and the median estimate is biased upward when many components are active (Appendix C ), which SURE compensates only in part. Explaining away is a single proximal step; it closes part of the gap to the joint code, and our synthetic study shows that it resolves redundancy in the code rather than disentangling the dictionary itself. Like every input-dependent adapter, Squelch cannot be merged into the backbone, and it adds a small inference overhead. Our experiments cover decoder models up to 14B parameters and one encoder, supervised fine-tuning, and English benchmarks; reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, multilingual adaptation, and larger models remain to be tested. Ethics Statement Squelch is a general fine-tuning method and inherits the risks of the models and data to which it is applied, including biases in instruction data and the lower cost of specializing models for harmful uses. All datasets are public and used under their licenses; no human subjects or personal data are involved. Because Squelch leaves out-of-domain tokens closer to the frozen model, it reduces but does not remove the risk that fine-tuning erodes safety behavior; such behavior should be evaluated after adaptation.
